claim: The inner ear has a rich population of pericytes.
source: The inner ear has a rich population of pericytes, a multi-functional mural cell essential for sensory hair cell heath and normal hearing.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by immunofluorescence imaging showing pericyte distribution in the cochlea.

claim: Pericytes are essential for sensory hair cell health and normal hearing.
source: The inner ear has a rich population of pericytes, a multi-functional mural cell essential for sensory hair cell heath and normal hearing.
evidence: This assertion is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing hearing loss after pericyte depletion.

claim: Pericyte depletion causes loss of vascular volume in the spiral ganglion.
source: In this study, using an inducible and conditional pericyte depletion mouse (PDGFRB-CreERT2; ROSA26iDTR) model, we demonstrate, for the first time, that pericyte depletion causes loss of vascular volume and spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs) and adversely affects hearing sensitivity.
evidence: Demonstrated through quantitative analysis of vascular density in pericyte-depleted mice showing significant reduction (Figure 2H).

claim: Pericyte depletion causes loss of spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs).
source: In this study, using an inducible and conditional pericyte depletion mouse (PDGFRB-CreERT2; ROSA26iDTR) model, we demonstrate, for the first time, that pericyte depletion causes loss of vascular volume and spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs) and adversely affects hearing sensitivity.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing significant SGN loss at all cochlear turns (Figure 4B: n=9, pApex=0.0085, pMid=0.0099, pBase=0.0127).

claim: Pericyte depletion adversely affects hearing sensitivity.
source: In this study, using an inducible and conditional pericyte depletion mouse (PDGFRB-CreERT2; ROSA26iDTR) model, we demonstrate, for the first time, that pericyte depletion causes loss of vascular volume and spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs) and adversely affects hearing sensitivity.
evidence: Demonstrated by ABR measurements showing significantly elevated hearing thresholds in pericyte-depleted animals (Figure 3A: n=10, p<0.0001).

claim: Pericytes markedly promote neurite growth in neonatal SGN explants.
source: Using an in vitro trans-well co-culture system, we show pericytes markedly promote neurite and vascular branch growth in neonatal SGN explants and adult SGNs.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-culture experiments showing significant differences in neurite number and length (Figure 5C: n=6, pNeurites #/area<0.0001, pNeurite length/explant=0.0393).

claim: Pericytes markedly promote vascular branch growth in neonatal SGN explants.
source: Using an in vitro trans-well co-culture system, we show pericytes markedly promote neurite and vascular branch growth in neonatal SGN explants and adult SGNs.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-culture experiments showing significant differences in vascular branch number (Figure 5C: n=6, pVascular branch #/area=0.0018).

claim: Pericyte-controlled neural growth is strongly mediated by pericyte-released exosomes containing VEGF-A.
source: The pericyte-controlled neural growth is strongly mediated by pericyte-released exosomes containing vascular endothelial growth factor-A (VEGF-A).
evidence: Supported by western blot showing VEGF-A in exosomes (Figure 7F), proteomic analysis identifying VEGF-A in exosomes, and functional experiments showing exosome effects are blocked by VEGFR2 inhibitor.

claim: Treatment of neonatal SGN explants with pericyte-derived exosomes significantly enhances angiogenesis.
source: Treatment of neonatal SGN explants or adult SGNs with pericyte-derived exosomes significantly enhances angiogenesis, SGN survival, and neurite growth, all of which were inhibited by a selective blocker of VEGF receptor 2 (Flk1).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis showing significant increase in vessel branches with exosome treatment (Figure 9D: n=6, p<0.0001).

claim: Treatment of neonatal SGN explants with pericyte-derived exosomes significantly enhances SGN survival.
source: Treatment of neonatal SGN explants or adult SGNs with pericyte-derived exosomes significantly enhances angiogenesis, SGN survival, and neurite growth, all of which were inhibited by a selective blocker of VEGF receptor 2 (Flk1).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis showing significant increase in neuron survival with exosome treatment (Figure 9E: n=4 wells, 25 cells per well, p=0.0048).

claim: Treatment of neonatal SGN explants with pericyte-derived exosomes significantly enhances neurite growth.
source: Treatment of neonatal SGN explants or adult SGNs with pericyte-derived exosomes significantly enhances angiogenesis, SGN survival, and neurite growth, all of which were inhibited by a selective blocker of VEGF receptor 2 (Flk1).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis showing significant increase in neurite number and length with exosome treatment (Figure 9D and 9E).

claim: The effects of pericyte-derived exosomes on angiogenesis, SGN survival, and neurite growth are inhibited by a selective blocker of VEGF receptor 2 (Flk1).
source: Treatment of neonatal SGN explants or adult SGNs with pericyte-derived exosomes significantly enhances angiogenesis, SGN survival, and neurite growth, all of which were inhibited by a selective blocker of VEGF receptor 2 (Flk1).
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments using SU5408 (VEGFR2 inhibitor) showing attenuation of exosome effects (Figure 9).

claim: Pericytes in the adult ear are critical for vascular stability.
source: Our study demonstrates that pericytes in the adult ear are critical for vascular stability and SGN health.
evidence: Demonstrated by loss of vascular volume and vascular shrinkage following pericyte depletion (Figure 2).

claim: Pericytes in the adult ear are critical for SGN health.
source: Our study demonstrates that pericytes in the adult ear are critical for vascular stability and SGN health.
evidence: Demonstrated by SGN loss and decreased β-III tubulin expression following pericyte depletion (Figure 4).

claim: Cross-talk between pericytes and SGNs via exosomes is essential for neuronal health.
source: Cross-talk between pericytes and SGNs via exosomes is essential for neuronal and vascular health and normal hearing.
evidence: Supported by observation of NG2-positive particles in SGN soma (Figure 1), exosome characterization, and functional experiments showing exosome effects on SGN survival and growth.

claim: Cross-talk between pericytes and SGNs via exosomes is essential for vascular health.
source: Cross-talk between pericytes and SGNs via exosomes is essential for neuronal and vascular health and normal hearing.
evidence: Supported by exosome effects on angiogenesis in SGN explants (Figure 9) and vascular loss following pericyte depletion (Figure 2).

claim: Cross-talk between pericytes and SGNs via exosomes is essential for normal hearing.
source: Cross-talk between pericytes and SGNs via exosomes is essential for neuronal and vascular health and normal hearing.
evidence: Supported by hearing loss following pericyte depletion (Figure 3) and the role of pericyte-derived exosomes in maintaining SGN and vascular health.

claim: The major microvascular network in the cochlea is located in the cochlear lateral wall.
source: The major microvascular network is located in the cochlear lateral wall, receiving ~80% of cochlear blood flow (Gyo, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Gyo, 2013.

claim: The cochlear lateral wall receives approximately 80% of cochlear blood flow.
source: The major microvascular network is located in the cochlear lateral wall, receiving ~80% of cochlear blood flow (Gyo, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Gyo, 2013.

claim: Blood flow to the cochlear lateral wall is essential for cochlear homeostasis.
source: Blood flow to the cochlear lateral wall is essential for cochlear homeostasis and is particularly important for generating the endocochlear potential necessary for sensory hair cell (HC) transduction (Hibino et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Hibino et al., 2010.

claim: Blood flow to the cochlear lateral wall is particularly important for generating the endocochlear potential necessary for sensory hair cell transduction.
source: Blood flow to the cochlear lateral wall is essential for cochlear homeostasis and is particularly important for generating the endocochlear potential necessary for sensory hair cell (HC) transduction (Hibino et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Hibino et al., 2010.

claim: The microvascular network in the spiral ganglion region comprises approximately 19-24% of cochlear blood flow.
source: The next largest microvascular network is situated in the region of the spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs), comprising ~19–24% of cochlear blood flow.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Angelborg et al., 1984; Gyo, 2013; Nakashima et al., 2001.

claim: The vascular network of the spiral ganglion is critical for neural activity.
source: The network is critical for neural activity (Angelborg et al., 1984; Gyo, 2013; Nakashima et al., 2001), in particular, the vascular network of the spiral ganglion directly delivers nutrients and growth hormones to SGNs (as illustrated in Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Angelborg et al., 1984; Gyo, 2013; Nakashima et al., 2001.

claim: The vascular network of the spiral ganglion directly delivers nutrients and growth hormones to SGNs.
source: The network is critical for neural activity (Angelborg et al., 1984; Gyo, 2013; Nakashima et al., 2001), in particular, the vascular network of the spiral ganglion directly delivers nutrients and growth hormones to SGNs (as illustrated in Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: Loss of SGNs is commonly associated with different types of hearing loss.
source: Loss of SGNs is commonly associated with different types of hearing loss (Leake et al., 2020; Viana et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Leake et al., 2020; Viana et al., 2015.

claim: Pericytes encircle endothelial cells of capillaries, pre-capillary arterioles, and post-capillary venules.
source: Pericytes are a type of mural cell that encircle endothelial cells of capillaries, pre-capillary arterioles, and post-capillary venules (Armulik et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Armulik et al., 2011.

claim: Pericytes play a critical role in regulating vascular morphogenesis and function.
source: They extend their processes along and around these vessels and play a critical role in regulating vascular morphogenesis and function (Attwell et al., 2016; Birbrair, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Attwell et al., 2016; Birbrair, 2018.

claim: Normal function of pericytes and adequate blood supply is crucial for providing vital oxygen, ions, and glucose to meet organ metabolic needs.
source: Normal function of pericytes and adequate blood supply is crucial for providing vital oxygen, ions, and glucose to meet organ metabolic needs (Shaw et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Shaw et al., 2018.

claim: Pericyte degeneration or loss has been identified as a major pathology in ischemic stroke.
source: Pericyte degeneration or loss has been identified as a major pathology in many diseases, including ischemic stroke (Greif and Eichmann, 2014), brain trauma (Zehendner et al., 2015), myocardial infarction (O'Farrell and Attwell, 2014), diabetic retinopathy (Pfister et al., 2008), and neurodegeneration diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Huntington's disease (Sweeney et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Greif and Eichmann, 2014.

claim: Pericyte degeneration or loss has been identified as a major pathology in brain trauma.
source: Pericyte degeneration or loss has been identified as a major pathology in many diseases, including ischemic stroke (Greif and Eichmann, 2014), brain trauma (Zehendner et al., 2015), myocardial infarction (O'Farrell and Attwell, 2014), diabetic retinopathy (Pfister et al., 2008), and neurodegeneration diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Huntington's disease (Sweeney et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Zehendner et al., 2015.

claim: Pericyte degeneration or loss has been identified as a major pathology in myocardial infarction.
source: Pericyte degeneration or loss has been identified as a major pathology in many diseases, including ischemic stroke (Greif and Eichmann, 2014), brain trauma (Zehendner et al., 2015), myocardial infarction (O'Farrell and Attwell, 2014), diabetic retinopathy (Pfister et al., 2008), and neurodegeneration diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Huntington's disease (Sweeney et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to O'Farrell and Attwell, 2014.

claim: Pericyte degeneration or loss has been identified as a major pathology in diabetic retinopathy.
source: Pericyte degeneration or loss has been identified as a major pathology in many diseases, including ischemic stroke (Greif and Eichmann, 2014), brain trauma (Zehendner et al., 2015), myocardial infarction (O'Farrell and Attwell, 2014), diabetic retinopathy (Pfister et al., 2008), and neurodegeneration diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Huntington's disease (Sweeney et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Pfister et al., 2008.

claim: Pericyte degeneration or loss has been identified as a major pathology in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Huntington's disease.
source: Pericyte degeneration or loss has been identified as a major pathology in many diseases, including ischemic stroke (Greif and Eichmann, 2014), brain trauma (Zehendner et al., 2015), myocardial infarction (O'Farrell and Attwell, 2014), diabetic retinopathy (Pfister et al., 2008), and neurodegeneration diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Huntington's disease (Sweeney et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Sweeney et al., 2018.

claim: Pericytes display phenotypic and functional heterogeneity, which is highly associated with organ function.
source: Pericytes are known to display phenotypic and functional heterogeneity, which is highly associated with organ function (Dias Moura Prazeres et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Dias Moura Prazeres et al., 2017.

claim: SGN cell bodies are located in Rosenthal's canal.
source: SGN cell bodies, located in Rosenthal's canal, extend distal processes radially outward into the spiral lamina toward sensory HCs in the organ of Corti and central processes project into the auditory nerve (as illustrated in Appendix 1—figure 1; Nayagam et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to Nayagam et al., 2011 and illustrated in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: SGNs extend distal processes radially outward into the spiral lamina toward sensory HCs in the organ of Corti.
source: SGN cell bodies, located in Rosenthal's canal, extend distal processes radially outward into the spiral lamina toward sensory HCs in the organ of Corti and central processes project into the auditory nerve (as illustrated in Appendix 1—figure 1; Nayagam et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to Nayagam et al., 2011 and illustrated in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: SGNs extend central processes that project into the auditory nerve.
source: SGN cell bodies, located in Rosenthal's canal, extend distal processes radially outward into the spiral lamina toward sensory HCs in the organ of Corti and central processes project into the auditory nerve (as illustrated in Appendix 1—figure 1; Nayagam et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to Nayagam et al., 2011 and illustrated in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: The microvascular network in the spiral ganglion region forms radial vascular twigs that directly supply nutrients to the SGNs.
source: The microvascular network, located in the spiral ganglion region, forms radial vascular twigs that directly supply nutrients to the SGNs.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an established anatomical fact.

claim: The volume of blood flow to the spiral lamina and SGN is lower than to the cochlear lateral wall.
source: Although the volume of blood flow to the spiral lamina and SGN is lower than to the cochlear lateral wall, it is critical for neuronal activity.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an established fact.

claim: Blood flow to the spiral lamina and SGN is critical for neuronal activity.
source: Although the volume of blood flow to the spiral lamina and SGN is lower than to the cochlear lateral wall, it is critical for neuronal activity.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an established fact.

claim: Constant sound stimulation to the inner ear imposes a high energy demand on neurons, requiring rapid delivery of oxygen and glucose.
source: Constant sound stimulation to the inner ear imposes a high energy demand on neurons, requiring rapid delivery of oxygen and glucose.
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference based on the metabolic demands of neuronal activity.

claim: The microvascular network in the spiral ganglion region is richly populated by pericytes.
source: Previously, we demonstrated the microvascular network in the spiral ganglion region is richly populated by pericytes (Jiang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citation to the authors' previous work (Jiang et al., 2019).

claim: Pericytes actively communicate with SGNs as evidenced by pericyte-released particles observed in the soma of SGNs.
source: Pericytes actively communicate with SGNs as evidenced by the pericyte-released particles observed in the soma of SGNs (Jiang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citation to the authors' previous work (Jiang et al., 2019) and supported by imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: Pericytes are predominantly distributed in the vascular bed of the spiral ganglion region.
source: Pericytes are predominantly distributed in the vascular bed, as shown in Figure 1A.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A confocal images.

claim: NG2-positive particles (likely released by pericytes) are observed in the soma of SGNs in NG2+ pericyte fluorescent reporter mice.
source: Most interestingly, in NG2+ pericyte fluorescent reporter mice, we observed NG2-positive particles (likely released by pericytes) in the soma of SGNs (Figure 1B lowest panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B, C, and D.

claim: Pericyte coverage in the vascular networks is significantly reduced in the spiral ganglion regions of all cochlear turns 2 weeks after DT treatment in CreERT2/iDTR mice.
source: Our results showed, relative to control mice, pericyte distribution (labeled with desmin) in the vascular networks (labeled with Alexa Fluor 649 conjugate lectin, a widely used fluorescence dye to visualize blood vessels [Meyer et al., 2008]), markedly reduced in the spiral ganglion regions of all cochlear turns 2 wk after DT treatment in the CreERT2/iDTR mice (n=5, pApex=0.0295, pMid=0.0361, pBase=0.005, unpaired t-test; Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis of pericyte coverage with statistical significance (Figure 2F).

claim: Vascular volume in the spiral ganglion region is notably reduced in pericyte-depleted mice.
source: In addition, the vascular volume in the spiral ganglion region was also notably reduced.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantitative data in Figure 2H.

claim: Total vascular density in the spiral lamina is significantly reduced in pericyte-depleted mice 2 weeks after DT injection.
source: Figure 2H shows total vascular density in the spiral lamina is significantly reduced in the pericyte-depleted mice 2 wk after DT injection (n=5, pApex=0.027, pMid=0.0108, pBase=0.0194, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis with statistical significance shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Vascular shrinkage, a sign of degeneration, is frequently observed in pericyte-depleted mice.
source: In addition, vascular shrinkage, a sign of degeneration, was frequently observed (as highlighted under high magnification, Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2G high magnification images.

claim: Control mice showed no significant hearing threshold change after DT injection.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, we found the control mice showed no significant hearing threshold change after DT injection.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A (n=10, p=0.9651).

claim: The hearing threshold in pericyte-depleted animals was significantly elevated at 1 week after DT injection and persisted to 2 weeks after DT injection.
source: In contrast, the hearing threshold in pericyte-depleted animals was significantly elevated at 1 wk after DT injection and persisted to 2 wk after DT injection (n=10, p<0.0001, two-way ANOVA), consistent with our previous observation (Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ABR measurements with statistical significance shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Control mice showed no significant wave I latency change after DT injection.
source: We found the control mice showed no significant wave I latency change after DT injection.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B (n=10, p=0.3576).

claim: Wave I latency in pericyte-depleted animals was significantly delayed at high frequency (32 kHz) starting with the fourth DT injection, and at low frequency (8 kHz) 2 weeks after DT injection.
source: In pericyte-depleted animals, the latency was significantly delayed at high frequency (32 kHz) starting with the fourth DT injection, and at low frequency (8 kHz) 2 wk after DT injection (n=10, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ABR wave I latency measurements with statistical significance shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Significant reduction in wave I amplitude was observed in pericyte-depleted animals at 2 weeks after DT injection, particularly at high frequency (32 kHz).
source: In contrast, significant reduction in wave I amplitude was observed in pericyte-depleted animals at 2 wk after DT injection, particularly at high frequency (32 kHz) (n=10, p8kHz<0.0001, p16kHz<0.0001, p24kHz<0.0001, p32kHz<0.0001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ABR wave I amplitude measurements with statistical significance shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Significant SGN loss was observed at all turns in pericyte-depleted animals 2 weeks after DT treatment.
source: In our pericyte-depleted animals, we observed significant SGN loss at all turns (Figure 4A and B; n=9, pApex=0.0085, pMid=0.0099, pBase=0.0127, unpaired t-test) with markedly decreased β-III tubulin expression 2 wk after DT treatment at the middle and basal turns (Figure 4A and C; pApex=0.1074, pMid<0.0001, pBase<0.0001, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis of SGN density with statistical significance shown in Figure 4B.

claim: β-III tubulin expression is markedly decreased in SGNs at the middle and basal turns 2 weeks after DT treatment in pericyte-depleted animals.
source: In our pericyte-depleted animals, we observed significant SGN loss at all turns (Figure 4A and B; n=9, pApex=0.0085, pMid=0.0099, pBase=0.0127, unpaired t-test) with markedly decreased β-III tubulin expression 2 wk after DT treatment at the middle and basal turns (Figure 4A and C; pApex=0.1074, pMid<0.0001, pBase<0.0001, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis of β-III tubulin intensity with statistical significance shown in Figure 4C.

claim: β-III tubulin is a specific marker for neuronal cytoskeleton commonly used to distinguish between different types of neurons.
source: β-III tubulin, a specific marker for neuronal cytoskeleton, is commonly used to distinguish between different types of neurons (Katsetos et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Katsetos et al., 2003.

claim: Reduced tubulin is an indication of structural disassembly seen in many neurodegenerative diseases and taken as a sign of neuronal dysfunction.
source: Reduced tubulin is an indication of structural disassembly seen in many neurodegenerative diseases and taken as a sign of neuronal dysfunction (Baas et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Baas et al., 2016.

claim: 12887 genes (RPKM>0) were identified as expressed in mouse cochlear pericytes by RNA-seq analysis.
source: 12887 genes (RPKM (reads per kilobase of exon per million reads mapped)>0) were identified expressed in mouse cochlear pericytes, 7889 (RPKM >0.5) of which were further analyzed by performing an overrepresentation test of Protein Analysis Through Evolutionary Relationships (PANTHER) pathways (relative to the whole-genome for Mus musculus) in the PANTHER classification system (version 17.0; Mi et al., 2013; Mi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated based on RNA-seq analysis of cochlear pericytes.

claim: 59 overrepresented PANTHER pathways were identified in the cochlear pericyte dataset.
source: We identified 59 overrepresented PANTHER pathways in our cochlear pericyte dataset (Table 1), including angiogenesis related ('CCKR signaling map,' P06959; 'Angiogenesis,' P00005; 'VEGF signaling pathway,' P00056) and neurodegeneration related ('Alzheimer disease-presenilin pathway,' P00004; 'Alzheimer disease-amyloid secretase pathway,' P00003; '5HT2 type receptor mediated signaling pathway,' P04374) pathways among the top 20 statistically significant results (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated based on PANTHER pathway analysis of RNA-seq data, shown in Table 1 and Figure 5A.

claim: Angiogenesis-related pathways are among the top 20 statistically significant overrepresented pathways in cochlear pericytes.
source: We identified 59 overrepresented PANTHER pathways in our cochlear pericyte dataset (Table 1), including angiogenesis related ('CCKR signaling map,' P06959; 'Angiogenesis,' P00005; 'VEGF signaling pathway,' P00056) and neurodegeneration related ('Alzheimer disease-presenilin pathway,' P00004; 'Alzheimer disease-amyloid secretase pathway,' P00003; '5HT2 type receptor mediated signaling pathway,' P04374) pathways among the top 20 statistically significant results (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated based on PANTHER pathway analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Neurodegeneration-related pathways are among the top 20 statistically significant overrepresented pathways in cochlear pericytes.
source: We identified 59 overrepresented PANTHER pathways in our cochlear pericyte dataset (Table 1), including angiogenesis related ('CCKR signaling map,' P06959; 'Angiogenesis,' P00005; 'VEGF signaling pathway,' P00056) and neurodegeneration related ('Alzheimer disease-presenilin pathway,' P00004; 'Alzheimer disease-amyloid secretase pathway,' P00003; '5HT2 type receptor mediated signaling pathway,' P04374) pathways among the top 20 statistically significant results (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated based on PANTHER pathway analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Neonatal SGN explants co-cultured with pericytes show robust SGN dendritic growth.
source: Neonatal spiral ganglion neuron (SGN) explants co-cultured with pericytes show robust SGN dendritic growth (green, labeled for β-III Tubulin) and new vessel growth (red, labeled for CD31).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Neonatal SGN explants co-cultured with pericytes show new vessel growth.
source: Neonatal spiral ganglion neuron (SGN) explants co-cultured with pericytes show robust SGN dendritic growth (green, labeled for β-III Tubulin) and new vessel growth (red, labeled for CD31).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There are significant differences in number of new vessel branches between pericyte co-cultured and control neonatal SGN explants.
source: There are significant differences in number of new vessel branches and in number and length of dendritic fibers in the two groups (n=6, pVascular branch #/area=0.0018, pNeurites #/area<0.0001, pNeurite length/explant=0.0393, unpaired t test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis with statistical significance shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There are significant differences in number of dendritic fibers between pericyte co-cultured and control neonatal SGN explants.
source: There are significant differences in number of new vessel branches and in number and length of dendritic fibers in the two groups (n=6, pVascular branch #/area=0.0018, pNeurites #/area<0.0001, pNeurite length/explant=0.0393, unpaired t test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis with statistical significance shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There are significant differences in length of dendritic fibers between pericyte co-cultured and control neonatal SGN explants.
source: There are significant differences in number of new vessel branches and in number and length of dendritic fibers in the two groups (n=6, pVascular branch #/area=0.0018, pNeurites #/area<0.0001, pNeurite length/explant=0.0393, unpaired t test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis with statistical significance shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Adult SGNs co-cultured with pericytes show robust SGN dendritic growth.
source: Adult SGNs co-cultured with pericytes show robust SGN dendritic growth (red, labeled for β-III Tubulin).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There are significant differences in cell survival between pericyte co-cultured and control adult SGNs.
source: There are significant differences in cell survival, and in average neurite number and length, in the two groups (n=3 wells per group, 25 cells per well, pneuron survival=0.0186, pNeurites #/cell<0.0001, plongest neurite length/cell<0.001, unpaired t test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis with statistical significance shown in Figure 5E.

claim: There are significant differences in average neurite number between pericyte co-cultured and control adult SGNs.
source: There are significant differences in cell survival, and in average neurite number and length, in the two groups (n=3 wells per group, 25 cells per well, pneuron survival=0.0186, pNeurites #/cell<0.0001, plongest neurite length/cell<0.001, unpaired t test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis with statistical significance shown in Figure 5E.

claim: There are significant differences in average neurite length between pericyte co-cultured and control adult SGNs.
source: There are significant differences in cell survival, and in average neurite number and length, in the two groups (n=3 wells per group, 25 cells per well, pneuron survival=0.0186, pNeurites #/cell<0.0001, plongest neurite length/cell<0.001, unpaired t test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis with statistical significance shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Exosomes are nano-sized 50-150 nm extracellular vesicles.
source: Most interestingly, we find the promotion of vascular and neuronal growth is mediated by pericyte-released exosomes, nano-sized 50–150 nm extracellular vesicles (EVs), containing vascular endothelial growth factor-A (VEGF-A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and confirmed by NTA analysis showing particle size distribution (Figure 6B).

claim: 96.4% of exosome-sized particles isolated from pericyte-conditioned media are labeled with Exoglow (a membrane EV marker kit).
source: Using nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), a widely employed technique for the characterization of particles in liquids (Dragovic et al., 2011), we found a rich population of exosome-sized (~50–150 nm) particles, 96.4% of which are labeled with Exoglow (a membrane EV marker kit), as shown in Figure 6B.
evidence: This is demonstrated by NTA analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Pericyte-derived exosomes show a classic cup-shaped structure consistent with previously described exosomes from other cell types.
source: Further transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images showed a classic cup-shaped structure in these membrane vesicles, which is consistent with previously described exosomes from other cell types, such as HCT116 cells (Jung and Mun, 2018) and utricles (Breglio et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in TEM images in Figure 6C.

claim: Proteomic analysis of purified pericyte-derived exosomes identified 580 proteins.
source: Moreover, proteomic analysis of purified pericyte-derived exosomes identified 580 proteins, 496 of which overlapped with genes that we identified in cochlear pericytes (Figure 6C), including the common exosome markers CD9, CD63, CD81, and Tsg101, as shown in Table 2.
evidence: This is stated based on proteomic analysis results shown in Figure 6D and Table 2.

claim: 496 proteins identified in pericyte-derived exosomes overlap with genes identified in cochlear pericytes.
source: Moreover, proteomic analysis of purified pericyte-derived exosomes identified 580 proteins, 496 of which overlapped with genes that we identified in cochlear pericytes (Figure 6C), including the common exosome markers CD9, CD63, CD81, and Tsg101, as shown in Table 2.
evidence: This is stated based on comparison of proteomic and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Common exosome markers CD9, CD63, CD81, and Tsg101 are present in pericyte-derived exosomes.
source: Moreover, proteomic analysis of purified pericyte-derived exosomes identified 580 proteins, 496 of which overlapped with genes that we identified in cochlear pericytes (Figure 6C), including the common exosome markers CD9, CD63, CD81, and Tsg101, as shown in Table 2.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Table 2 with specific protein identification data.

claim: GO enrichment analysis identified 22 enriched cellular component terms for proteins in pericyte-derived exosomes, including 'extracellular exosomes'.
source: Analysis by cellular component class identified enrichment of 22 GO terms, including 'extracellular exosomes' (GO: 0070062), neurotransmission related terms such as 'myelin sheath' (GO: 0043209) and 'presynaptic membrane' (GO: 0042734) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated based on GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Angiogenesis-related pathways are among the top ranks of PANTHER pathways identified in pericyte-derived exosome proteins.
source: Although analysis by PANTHER pathways did not identify significantly enriched pathways, we listed the identified pathways in the order of relative protein number (Figure 6E) and found that the angiogenesis related ('Angiogenesis,' P00005; 'VEGF signaling pathway,' P00056) and neurodegeneration related ('Parkinson disease,' P00049; 'Huntington disease,' P00029) pathways were among the top ranks.
evidence: This is stated based on PANTHER pathway analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Neurodegeneration-related pathways are among the top ranks of PANTHER pathways identified in pericyte-derived exosome proteins.
source: Although analysis by PANTHER pathways did not identify significantly enriched pathways, we listed the identified pathways in the order of relative protein number (Figure 6E) and found that the angiogenesis related ('Angiogenesis,' P00005; 'VEGF signaling pathway,' P00056) and neurodegeneration related ('Parkinson disease,' P00049; 'Huntington disease,' P00029) pathways were among the top ranks.
evidence: This is stated based on PANTHER pathway analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: VEGF-A is expressed in cochlear pericytes as identified by bulk RNA-seq analysis.
source: Our bulk RNA-seq analysis identified VEGF-A expression in cochlea pericytes, as did RT-PCR (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated based on RNA-seq and RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Pericytes release 3.696±0.003 ng of VEGF-A per 8 × 10^5 cells into 4 ml of culture medium without growth factors after 3 days of culture.
source: ELISA protein analysis showed 3.696±0.003 ng of VEGF-A/ 8 × 105 pericytes released into 4 ml of culture medium without growth factors after 3 d culture (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Significantly less VEGF-A is produced in the cochlea when pericytes are depleted in vivo.
source: In contrast, when we depleted the pericytes in vivo, we found significantly less production of VEGF-A in the cochlea (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA analysis comparing control and pericyte-depleted cochleae shown in Figure 7C (ncontrol = 5, npericyte depletion=8, p=0.0387).

claim: VEGF-A is expressed in pericytes in the spiral ganglion region.
source: The immunofluorescence staining further corroborated the VEGFA expression in pericytes in the spiral ganglion region (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Both PDGFRβ and VEGF-A are expressed in exosomes but not detected in the non-exosomal supernatant fraction.
source: We found that both PDGFRβ (a pericyte cellular membrane marker) and VEGF-A were expressed in the exosomes but not detected in the non-exosomal supernatant fraction (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: VEGFR2 is expressed in both SGNs and blood vessels in the cochlea.
source: We used immunofluorescence to identify VEGFR2 expression in both SGNs and blood vessels, as shown in Figure 8A–D.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 8A-D.

claim: Exosome treatment promotes vascular growth in neonatal SGN explants, which is attenuated by the specific VEGFR2 inhibitor SU5408 at 100 nM.
source: We found the exosome treatment promoted both vascular and neuronal growth in neonatal SGN explants, which was attenuated by the specific VEGFR2 inhibitor, SU5408 (Roskoski, 2017) at 100 nM (n=6, pVascular branch #/area<0.0001; pNeurites #/area<0.0001; pNeurites #/area=0.0268, one-way ANOVA; Figure 9B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis with statistical significance shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Exosome treatment promotes neuronal growth in neonatal SGN explants, which is attenuated by the specific VEGFR2 inhibitor SU5408 at 100 nM.
source: We found the exosome treatment promoted both vascular and neuronal growth in neonatal SGN explants, which was attenuated by the specific VEGFR2 inhibitor, SU5408 (Roskoski, 2017) at 100 nM (n=6, pVascular branch #/area<0.0001; pNeurites #/area<0.0001; pNeurites #/area=0.0268, one-way ANOVA; Figure 9B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis with statistical significance shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Exosome treatment promotes survival of adult SGNs, which is arrested by SU5408.
source: Similarly, exosome treatment also promoted the survival and neurite growth of adult SGNs, which was also arrested by SU5408 (n=4 wells, 25 cells per well, pcell survial=0.0048, pNeurites #/cell<0.0001, plongest neurite length/cell<0.0001, one-way ANOVA; Figure 9C and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis with statistical significance shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Exosome treatment promotes neurite growth of adult SGNs, which is arrested by SU5408.
source: Similarly, exosome treatment also promoted the survival and neurite growth of adult SGNs, which was also arrested by SU5408 (n=4 wells, 25 cells per well, pcell survial=0.0048, pNeurites #/cell<0.0001, plongest neurite length/cell<0.0001, one-way ANOVA; Figure 9C and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis with statistical significance shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Pericyte-derived exosomes promote vascular and neuronal growth through a VEGFA/VEGFR2 signaling pathway.
source: The results indicate pericyte-derived exosomes promote vascular and neuronal growth through a VEGFA/VEGFR2 signaling pathway.
evidence: This is concluded based on experiments showing exosome effects are blocked by VEGFR2 inhibitor (Figure 9).

claim: Loss of pericytes in the CNS causes brain infarction with diminished capillary perfusion and blood flow.
source: In the CNS, loss of pericytes causes brain infarction with diminished capillary perfusion and blood flow (Armulik et al., 2010; Bell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Armulik et al., 2010; Bell et al., 2010.

claim: Damaged pericytes in the mouse brain effectively constrict capillaries and induce a long-lasting reduction in cerebral blood flow.
source: In the mouse brain, damaged pericytes effectively constrict capillaries and induce a long-lasting reduction in cerebral blood flow, even after recanalization of the larger vessels, and it causes a no-reflow condition (Hall et al., 2014; Kloner et al., 2018; Yemisci et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Hall et al., 2014; Kloner et al., 2018; Yemisci et al., 2009.

claim: Loss of pericytes interrupts blood-brain-barrier integrity.
source: Loss of pericytes also interrupts blood-brain-barrier integrity (Armulik et al., 2010; Bell et al., 2010; Nikolakopoulou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Armulik et al., 2010; Bell et al., 2010; Nikolakopoulou et al., 2019.

claim: Pericytes control perfusion of cochlear blood flow.
source: In peripheral organs such as the ear, we previously reported that pericytes control perfusion of cochlear blood flow (Dai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citation to the authors' previous work (Dai et al., 2010).

claim: Loss of pericytes leads to increased cochlear permeability and reduced endocochlear potential.
source: Loss of pericytes leads to increased cochlear permeability and reduced endocochlear potential (Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with citation to the authors' previous work (Zhang et al., 2021).

claim: The tdTomato fluorescence signal largely co-localized with the immunofluorescence signal for PDGFRβ in the vascular networks of PDGFRB-CreERT2; ROSA26tdTomato mice.
source: As expected, the tdTomato fluorescence signal (Greenhalgh et al., 2013) largely co-localized with the immunofluorescence signal for the pericyte marker protein, PDGFRβ (green) in the vascular networks, as shown in Figure 2C and D.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: PDGFR-β is expressed by all cochlear pericytes.
source: However, PDGFR-β is a general membrane protein not only expressed by all cochlear pericytes (Canis and Bertlich, 2019; Shi et al., 2008) but also by pericytes in other organs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Canis and Bertlich, 2019; Shi et al., 2008.

claim: Pericytes display considerable phenotypic and functional heterogeneity in different tissues and organs.
source: The different results obtained from pericyte depletion does, however, support the notion that pericytes display considerable phenotypic and functional heterogeneity in different tissues and organs (Sims, 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Sims, 2000.

claim: SGNs are neural elements transmitting localized electrical activity from HCs to second-order neurons in the cochlear nucleus.
source: SGNs are neural elements transmitting localized electrical activity from HCs to second-order neurons in the cochlear nucleus (Coate et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Coate et al., 2019.

claim: Pericyte loss triggers primary vascular dysfunction, leading to neurodegeneration.
source: It is well-documented that pericyte loss triggers primary vascular dysfunction, leading to neurodegeneration (Winkler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Winkler et al., 2011.

claim: In the CNS, pericyte loss induces vascular leakage, insufficient blood perfusion, and tissue hypoxia, ultimately leading to neuron degeneration.
source: For example, in the CNS, pericyte loss induces vascular leakage, insufficient blood perfusion, and tissue hypoxia, ultimately leading to neuron degeneration (Quaegebeur et al., 2010; Sagare et al., 2013; Winkler et al., 2011; Zlokovic, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Quaegebeur et al., 2010; Sagare et al., 2013; Winkler et al., 2011; Zlokovic, 2011.

claim: SGNs are vulnerable to interruption of the blood supply since the energy demand of SGNs is directly met by the surrounding blood circulation.
source: SGNs are vulnerable to interruption of the blood supply since the energy demand of SGNs is directly met by the surrounding blood circulation (Jiang et al., 2019; Mei et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Jiang et al., 2019; Mei et al., 2020.

claim: Pericyte loss induces capillary rarefaction in acute kidney injury.
source: Our data is supported by Kramann et al., where it was found pericyte loss induces capillary rarefaction in acute kidney injury (Guzmán-Hernández et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Guzmán-Hernández et al., 2014 (note: this appears to be a citation error in the original manuscript).

claim: Detachment of pericytes from endothelial cells can interrupt cross-talk signaling and destabilize capillaries.
source: Detachment of pericytes from endothelial cells can interrupt cross-talk signaling and destabilize capillaries, as we earlier reported (Hou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citation to the authors' previous work (Hou et al., 2020).

claim: Without the presence of pericytes, tight junction adhesive proteins such as ZO-1 are significantly reduced.
source: Without the presence of pericytes, tight junction adhesive proteins such as ZO-1 are significantly reduced (Neng et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is stated with citation to the authors' previous work (Neng et al., 2013b).

claim: Pericytes release many growth factors relevant to maintenance of organ homeostasis.
source: Pericytes release many growth factors relevant to maintenance of organ homeostasis (Gaceb et al., 2018a; Gaceb et al., 2018b; Gaceb and Paul, 2018c).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Gaceb et al., 2018a; Gaceb et al., 2018b; Gaceb and Paul, 2018c.

claim: Exosomes transport cargo such as nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids and have significant physiological effects in recipient cells.
source: Many cells release exosomes, nano-sized EVs (50–150 nm diameter), which transport cargo such as nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids. These exosomes have significant physiological effects in the recipient cells (Bang and Thum, 2012; Colombo et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Bang and Thum, 2012; Colombo et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: Pericyte-released exosomes were first reported by Gaceb and Paul, 2018c.
source: Pericyte-released exosomes were first reported by Gaceb and Paul, 2018c.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Gaceb and Paul, 2018c.

claim: Pericyte-derived exosomes participate in regulation of microvascular function under different pathological conditions.
source: However recent studies have amply demonstrated that pericyte-derived exosomes participate in regulation of microvascular function under different pathological conditions (Ye et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Ye et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2019.

claim: VEGF/VEGFR2 signaling plays a critical role in both angiogenesis and neuroprotection.
source: VEGF/VEGFR2 signaling is a well-defined, classical pathway that plays a critical role in both angiogenesis and neuroprotection (Storkebaum and Carmeliet, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Storkebaum and Carmeliet, 2004.

claim: VEGFR2 is typically expressed in both vascular cells and SGNs.
source: VEGFR2 is typically expressed in both vascular cells and SGNs (Figure 8A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 8A-D.

claim: Blockage of the VEGFR2 receptor with SU5408 dramatically halts angiogenesis in SGN explants.
source: Our results show blockage of the VEGFR2 receptor with a specific VEGFR2 inhibitor, SU5408 (Roskoski, 2017), dramatically halts angiogenesis and neuronal growth (Figure 9), indicating that pericyte-derived VEGF-A-containing exosomes promote both vascular and neuronal growth through a VGFR2 signaling pathway.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: Blockage of the VEGFR2 receptor with SU5408 dramatically halts neuronal growth in SGN explants.
source: Our results show blockage of the VEGFR2 receptor with a specific VEGFR2 inhibitor, SU5408 (Roskoski, 2017), dramatically halts angiogenesis and neuronal growth (Figure 9), indicating that pericyte-derived VEGF-A-containing exosomes promote both vascular and neuronal growth through a VGFR2 signaling pathway.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: Treatment with the VEGFR2 inhibitor almost completely blocked the effect of exosomes relative to control groups.
source: However, it must be emphasized that treatment with the VEGFR2 inhibitor almost completely blocked the effect of the exosomes relative to control groups (see Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 9.

claim: VEGF-A/VEGFR2 signaling is the dominant factor regulating vascular and neuronal growth in the context of pericyte-derived exosomes.
source: This suggests the VEGF-A/VEGFR2 signaling is the dominant factor regulating vascular and neuronal growth.
evidence: This is concluded based on the near-complete blockade of exosome effects by VEGFR2 inhibitor (Figure 9).

claim: Loss of pericytes disrupts vascular structure and damages SGNs.
source: In summary, our data provide the first clear-cut experimental evidence that pericytes are essential for the maintenance of cochlear vascular stability and SGN viability in adults. Loss of pericytes disrupts vascular structure and damages SGNs.
evidence: This is concluded based on the experimental data showing vascular loss and SGN damage following pericyte depletion.

claim: The damage from pericyte loss is related to the impairment of VEGF-A mediated communication between pericytes, endothelial cells, and SGNs.
source: The damage is related to the impairment of VEGF-A mediated communication between pericytes, endothelial cells, and SGNs, as illustrated in Figure 11.
evidence: This is concluded based on the experimental data showing VEGF-A in exosomes and the effects of VEGFR2 inhibition, illustrated in Figure 11.

claim: Pericyte-released exosomes have a major role in vascular and neuronal health.
source: These findings demonstrate for the first time that pericyte-released exosomes have a major role in vascular and neuronal health.
evidence: This is concluded based on the experimental data showing exosome effects on angiogenesis, SGN survival, and neurite growth.

claim: A dose-dependent relationship exists between SU5408 concentration and neurite number and length in pericyte-SGN explant co-culture.
source: Number and length of dendritic fibers when the VEGFR2 receptor is blocked. A dose-dependent relationship is shown (n=3, pnumber<0.0001, plength<0.0001, one-way ANOVA followed by a Tukey's multiple comparison test, individual p values between different groups labeled on the graph).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dose-response experiments shown in Figure 10.
